> So if you set the constraint priority to 1000, then that constraint will actually be solved `1000 * iterations` times, which will be insanely slow. Note that the UI limits the max value to 8, but I think you can set it to any value if you script it.
> Jolt on the other hand uses the priority only to sort the constraints, so all constraints will be solved `iterations` times, but the highest priority joints are solved last which means that they will be solved more accurately (the first constraints can be violated when solving the last constraints).

Wow... so basically if someone assumes the sorting strategy (which is how the concept of "priority" should be handled), and increments their joints as they create them, switching to Godot physics would probably instantly crash any project with more than 10 constraints.

> I think the tool tip needs to be adjusted to:
> 
>  - Reflect that higher values have a higher priority.
>  - Remove the note that Jolt doesn't support it.

Yes, I agree. I forgot to update the documentation.

> As you can pass an int to the `set_solver_priority` function and it is cast to an unsigned integer, I think the value set should be `max(0, value)`.

Initially when I was using priorities, I had the idea to start at `-1` and decrement a `priority` variable as I set up my joints. This basically has the intention of making joints created A, B, C run as C, B, A. I'm not sure of where compilers may differ, but it should probably be supported to use negative numbers as a strategy to say "maximum priority" minus 1, then minus 2, etc. Maybe this is crazy. Personally though, I like the option.

I saw that Jolt runs with uints, and I didn't confirm it, but I was running with "negative" priorities assuming the cast will underflow. It probably wasn't though. Whatever way, the doc should mention what happens with negative values, as normal ints in GDScript are always signed.

@jrouwe about the need to update the priority on each joint individually, I actually remembered seeing this shouldn't be needed because from the outside, everything is a Joint3D, and Joint3D always sets the priority after running `_configure_joint()`. Do you agree that this ensures the priority will match? When changing it directly, the setter already passes it to the physics `JoltJoint3D` which directly sets it on the constraint.

The specific line here is 108, which leads to the code already written.

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/f92a322ad49811f608146750a40fcb31439f24d2/scene/3d/physics/joints/joint_3d.cpp#L99-L109

However, I am not exactly a fan of the code duplication, every jolt joint does the same two things when reconfiguring, confusing any dev about where some logic should actually go:

https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/ec67cbe92628bdaf979b10594359ba6f02cf8838/modules/jolt_physics/joints/jolt_generic_6dof_joint_3d.cpp#L672-L673

I have a version right now that adds `_update_priority()`, but that was really starting to look terrible so I also move all three to a new `_update_joint()` method which just calls all three methods, and that method is now replacing this part on all joints. Do you have any ideas for how to just pull these entirely out of the individual joints and move them to the main `Joint3D._configure_joint()` method? It would require adding iterations to the PhysicsServer3D API I think... but now this PR would be getting a little large with not-so-relevant changes.

I've created a MRP where the constraint priority is lost:

[hinge-test.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/28912987/hinge-test.zip)

The trick is this script:

```GDScript
extends Node3D

@onready var hinge: HingeJoint3D = $HingeJoint3D

func _physics_process(delta: float) -> void:
	hinge.set_param(HingeJoint3D.PARAM_LIMIT_LOWER, deg_to_rad(-90.0))
```

When changing the limits of the hinge we enter `JoltHingeJoint3D::set_param` which updates the limits and then calls `JoltHingeJoint3D::_limits_changed` which will call `JoltHingeJoint3D::rebuild`. This will destroy and recreate the constraint at which point the constraint priority is 0 again. If you put a breakpoint in `PhysicsSystem::Update` and inspect `mConstraintManager.mConstraints[0].mPtr->mConstraintPriority` you'll see that it is still 0 during simulation (it is configured to 4 and when we enter `JoltHingeJoint3D::set_param` then `jolt_ref->mConstraintPriority` is still 4).

I've been sitting on some changes, especially with making the rest of the joints actually configure the priorities. I can clearly see the route that bypasses the normal `Joint3D::_update_joint()` method, normal calls to the PhysicsServer3D can destroy joints and recreate them. While I think it's crazy to destroy and reallocate a joint when it could have just been changing the struct member, I suppose the easiest thing is to just get with the flow and add the priority configuration to the rebuild methods. There could be stability concerns with lambdas but I think that's acceptable if a developer is changing a constraint parameter at runtime.

I already wrote all that, though, just wanted to be totally sure about it before sending.

> I've created a MRP where the constraint priority is lost

Just tested on the new patch, pulling priority with `PhysicsServer3D.joint_get_solver_priority(hinge.get_rid())` before and after changing the angle limit, and both returned `4`.
